# In Praise of the Wrong Turn

A wrong turn is a fact; wrongness is a verdict. The road does not announce that we have gone astray. It simply continues beneath our feet, past a junction we did not notice, toward a place we had not chosen. Only afterward, perhaps after unfolding a map or hearing a local describe the distance to our destination, do we begin to construct the story of error. The turn acquires a name. The journey becomes a mistake. Yet for a while, the traveler has merely been moving through the world, and the world has been under no obligation to confirm expectations.

This is worth defending: the value of getting lost, taking the wrong path, and allowing a plan to meet something it cannot entirely absorb. We live amid increasingly confident instructions. A device tells us which lane to take, how many minutes remain, where the entrance is. Maps promise to shrink the uncertain world into a clean arrangement of lines. Schedules divide the day into blocks that appear to have already succeeded or failed. Even our desires are encouraged to become targets, measurable outcomes waiting to be optimized. Against this, the wrong turn offers a small but genuine freedom: the possibility that the route might be more interesting than the plan.

Childhood maps are often terrible. They are drawn on paper that stretches, fold after fold, until the names become faint and the colors bleed together. A blue line meant to be a river wanders into a yellow neighborhood. A child places a house where a mountain should be, not from carelessness but from an assumption that scale can be negotiated. The map is not chiefly a record of distance. It is a picture of what mattered: the bakery with the blue door, the field where a dog waited, the corner around which too many turns had made everyone disappear. To be lost inside such a map is not to fail at geography. It is to discover that the important features have not been marked.

Adults tend to replace imaginative maps with correct ones. A child who wanders is brought safely home; a child who draws the world incorrectly is gently taught to draw it again. Somewhere along the way, the correction becomes a habit of thought. We learn to identify the wrong answer quickly, perhaps before fully understanding the question. Certainty becomes a form of comfort, and discomfort becomes evidence that something has gone wrong. Yet many valuable things begin as apparent errors: the unfamiliar observation, the awkward metaphor, the question that sounds foolish until it proves more accurate than the polished one.

Science, despite its reputation for precision, is full of wrong turns. Important discoveries often begin with a result that looks disappointing. A culture is ignored because it does not behave like mold. A substance is dismissed because its effect is inconsistent. A mathematical proof reaches a dead end, and the mathematician is forced to discover that the problem, rather than the argument, was misunderstood. The eventual solution does not erase the false starts. It incorporates them, turning them into signs of the question’s depth.

One of the most famous stories in modern medicine concerns a contaminated culture plate. Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold had invaded one of his petri dishes and that the bacteria around it had disappeared. Instead of treating this as ruined work, he asked what the mold had done. Penicillin became the answer, though many years of difficult work were required before it could become medicine. The familiar retelling makes the discovery look like a stroke of luck. Less emphasized is the initial wrongness: something that did not belong where it was supposed to belong, creating a condition no one had requested. The laboratory became fertile ground because it contained an interruption.

Not every interruption is fertile. A person can take a wrong turn away from safety, away from responsibilities, away from obligations they genuinely owe. It would be too simple to celebrate error merely because it makes a better story. The world is not arranged as a classroom in which every mistake carries a lesson. Sometimes a road is closed. Sometimes a supposed detour exhausts us. Sometimes the lesson is simply to turn back. Humility is not the same as passivity, and curiosity does not require us to treat every danger as an opportunity for growth.

Still, the habit of seeing every deviation as failure makes an anxious relationship with the world. It turns experience into a series of audits. We are always checking whether our location matches the approved one. We become reluctant to linger anywhere that cannot justify itself in advance. A walk must produce a step count, a book must yield a useful lesson, a conversation must reach a conclusion. The afternoon in which nothing is accomplished begins to feel like time stolen from a more serious purpose.

Getting lost can restore a missing sense of proportion. Stand in an unfamiliar street at dusk and the apparent hierarchy of places often rearranges itself. A narrow doorway may glow more warmly than the imposing avenue. A bakery may be exactly where everyone stops for coffee, though it appears on no tourist map. A public garden may contain one bench occupied by someone reading a newspaper, and the quiet endurance of that person may become more memorable than any famous building. Without a destination to organize attention, the street becomes briefly itself: a collection of sounds, weather, gestures, and chances.

Cities are especially good at this when their plans fail them. Look above the oldest rooftops and the towers no longer line up. Older paths survive beneath newer paving. A lane that once carried carts now carries pedestrians, but it still bends for a reason. Lost travelers sometimes discover these continuities. They see that a city is not a diagram imposed once upon empty land. It is a negotiation among generations, each leaving a groove that the next may misunderstand. The wrong turn can reveal history more honestly than the direct route.

There is also a forgotten quality in being unable to find a particular shop because the street has changed. The building remains, but its role has shifted. The bakery has become a pharmacy; the cinema has become a supermarket; the little hotel now contains a restaurant with a different name. We expected a landscape to hold still while we returned to it. Instead, the place has moved on without permission. Anyone who has searched for a former home experiences this with particular force. The street seems to insist, *You said this was where you belonged*. The building answers, *I have been here, but not in the way you remember*.

Maps are therefore more than tools of navigation. They are arguments about what deserves attention. They privilege the road that is easiest to travel and the landmark that is easiest to name. A village may appear as a small dot; a border may appear as a thin line, though it can contain languages, histories, and grief. Indigenous peoples have developed forms of mapping that center routes, seasons, stories, relationships, and responsibilities rather than fixed coordinates. To call these maps “wrong” because they do not resemble a cadastral plan is to mistake our categories for the world’s necessities.

To become properly lost, then, is partly to discover that orientation is not always a matter of north and south. One can be deeply oriented toward a responsibility, a person, a season, or a way of understanding, while being geographically uncertain. One can know exactly where one belongs and still be unsure how to arrive. Conversely, a traveler may know no landmarks and still possess a remarkably clear sense of direction. The inner compass and the outer one do not always agree.

Children seem to understand this instinctively. Give a child a box, a few ordinary objects, and an hour, and a kingdom appears. A chair becomes a boat. A blanket becomes a roof. The space under a table becomes a cave with laws of its own. Nothing needs to be useful in the ordinary sense. An object can be something else entirely because play has declared a new possibility. Adults often admire this imaginative freedom while quietly arranging their lives to prevent its return. We furnish the room with the correct furniture, schedule the correct tasks, and call it adulthood as though imagination had been successfully contained.

Play is not an escape from seriousness. It is a way of taking the world apart without being frightened by what might emerge. The wrong turn belongs to the same family. It unsettles the expected arrangement and makes another arrangement briefly visible. That is why a good mistake can be so unsettling. Once we have imagined an alternative, we cannot quite see the original plan as inevitable. The room contains more doors than we noticed. The road contains more directions than the map admits.

Conversation offers a quieter version of the same experience. There are moments when one person says something that seems beside the point, and another person, impatient to return to the argument, misses the hidden doorway. To listen without immediately translating the statement into agreement or disagreement is a kind of getting lost. It allows the conversation to become larger than its original destination. Many friendships are maintained not by perfect understanding but by the patience to discover that the person beside us is not entirely where either of us placed them.

The same applies to stories. A plot may take an unexpected turn, and readers sometimes protest that it has violated the rules established on the first page. But the rules of a story are not laws of reality. The unexpected turn is often where the work begins to discover what it is about. A character makes the wrong decision, and the consequences expose an emotion the author had not consciously recognized. A novel goes somewhere other than its intended ending, and the writer is obliged to follow it. Sometimes the finished work contains a door the architect did not remember building.

This is why the first drafts of so many things are valuable. They are not judged by their fidelity to the final form. They are records of a mind finding its way. A sentence that seems too loud may be carrying an important piece of energy. An image that initially appears unrelated may belong to a pattern not yet visible. The apparent mistake has not yet become meaningful, but neither has the whole. To discard everything unfamiliar is to preserve only the part of the imagination that already knows how to behave.

Art and science require different kinds of error. A scientist can test a false hypothesis and learn precisely why it fails. An artist may keep a false image because its emotional accuracy exceeds its factual accuracy. Both practices become impoverished when every wrongness is treated identically. A beautiful map can be false, and an accurate account of a landscape can be dull. The point is not that every route is equally good. The point is that we need enough room to discover which route deserves to continue.

There is a practical wisdom in all this. Leave a little space in the day. When a train is late, do not immediately calculate the loss. When a meeting ends early, resist the urge to fill every available minute with another task. When a conversation takes an unexpected turn, stay long enough to hear what it is saying. These are small forms of wrongness: departures from the schedule, the agenda, the route that was supposed to be efficient. They can feel uncomfortable at first because efficiency has trained us to treat spare time as an unfinished task.

But rest is not a failure of purpose. Boredom can restore the mind’s ability to notice. When there is nothing urgent demanding interpretation, the mind begins making quieter connections. A shadow resembles the handle of a cup. A forgotten word returns with a different meaning. A person across the room makes a gesture that belongs in an old story. The world does not become less ordinary, but ordinary things recover their depth. Attention, given no other work to do, becomes capable of seeing more.

The morning after a period of constant urgency is often like walking through a familiar neighborhood in a dream. The street is unchanged, yet its scale has altered. A gate you passed every day reveals spikes you never noticed. A tree has been quietly growing behind a wall. The hours have been full, but the days have felt thin. Getting lost in time can be a way of recovering proportion. It reminds us that a life is not only a sequence of completed objectives, but also the spaces in which the consequences of those objectives become visible.

A person can be geographically lost without being physically in danger. The distinction matters. Some landscapes deserve respect, and some mistakes deserve correction. Do not make a virtue of confusion when clarity would protect another person. Do not call cruelty a necessary detour merely because it leads somewhere unexpected. Do not confuse a refusal to learn with an openness to possibility. The wrong turn becomes worthwhile when it is approached with curiosity rather than used to excuse carelessness.

Even the phrase “getting lost” hides a little shame. It suggests that a competent person should have known better. Yet the world is far too large, complicated, and changeable for competence to mean certainty. Anyone who claims to know exactly what they are doing is usually describing a small section of the journey. The rest remains unmapped. A useful humility is the willingness to admit that our instructions have limits, and that reaching a dead end may simply mean the map was made for another kind of traveler.

The best maps include blank spaces. They show the known world while admitting that knowledge has edges. To be lost is to enter one of those spaces without immediately demanding that it become another boundary, another label, another certainty. It is to permit the unknown to remain unknown for a while. The point is not to cultivate ignorance. The point is to avoid confusing the limits of our knowledge with the limits of reality.

Consider a traveler who leaves a familiar city with no plan beyond walking in one direction. By evening, the route has become difficult to describe. There is a bakery, a canal, a bridge with a cracked railing, a child flying a kite in a field no one else is using. None of these places was the destination. Together, however, they have produced a day that cannot be exchanged for any more efficient one. The traveler has not accomplished something measurable. They have simply been present in a world that was not waiting to be conquered.

Now imagine the same traveler refusing every deviation because the original plan matters more than the day itself. They reach the destination on schedule. They complete the task. They return home with the satisfaction of having avoided error. Yet the route has been reduced to a means, and the places encountered along it have become obstacles. The traveler has arrived, but in what sense? The journey has been completed without necessarily having been lived.

A wrong turn interrupts that reduction. It says: there is more here than the purpose that brought you. It may still be necessary to return to the plan. The meeting must happen, the train must be caught, the bill must be paid. But the detour has left a mark. It has made the traveler a person who knows that the world contains rooms not included in the itinerary.

At the end of a life, we may remember not the routes that made us most efficient, but the moments when we were forced to reconsider. The afternoon we missed the last bus. The friend who asked an unexpected question. The child who saw an animal in the hedge. The place we entered without knowing why. The error became a hinge, and the life swung open.

So perhaps the next time a road seems to be going nowhere, let it go a little farther. Not recklessly, not forever, and not without regard to the people depending on your return. Take the turn early enough to remain safe. Walk slowly enough to see what is beside the road. Listen for the sound of a place that did not appear on the map. Later, if the detour proves useless, call it what it was: a wrong turn. But do not confuse being wrong with having wasted the day.

The road does not owe us a revelation. It may lead only to a locked gate, a muddy field, a view of a warehouse. Still, the traveler has learned something about the difference between intention and result. A plan can be good without being exhaustive. A mistake can occur without becoming a disaster. And the direction we thought was necessary may, from another angle, have been the first permission to look around.

Ultimately, the wrong turn is not an argument against maps. It is a reminder that the map is not the territory, that even the territory is larger than our description, and that a person is not lost merely because they are somewhere they did not intend to be. Sometimes the road is not leading us away from where we meant to go. It is bringing us, slowly and by an unforeseen route, toward what we did not know how to ask for.
